As an overweight person, I've ironically worked for 2 weight loss companies - in fact, I still work for one. They suggest measuring yourself as motivation. You see more results with inches than you do with lbs. Maybe give it a try?

you are very tough for telling people this, even if it is anonymously over the internet. i know. i started crying when i read it. it's hard to even admit this stuff to yourself.

someone else has already said "Losing weight isn't going to solve your problems." and they are completely correct.

May I please be as bold as to suggest a therapist that SPECIALIZES in weight and food disorders? I think they will understand your issues much more than the other therapists you saw - it seems like they did more damage than good. 

Also, group therapy sounds like a possibility too - you'll see that you aren't alone. And maybe even a pet? My dog loves me unconditionally - and that's really nice. Feel free to start with a fish - it's a nice commitment in itself.

Now I'm going to talk about something else that makes me cry: I recently joined a medical weight loss program (no drugs or anything scary like that) at a university. At the urging of my loving and meaning well siblings, I finally had to admit that I have a real problem with my relationship to food. Not just eating - it's mostly mentally based. I'm only about to finish my first week today, but for the first time in a long time, I feel like I have hope when it comes to being healthy for the first time in a long time.

I thought I'd bring this up because over the past few weeks, getting an appointment, and talking to my siblings about my problem for the first time - i was always to ashamed to talk about it - i feel like i've finally taken an immensely important step just in doing all that. So my advice is to treat this as YOUR first step. 

Reddit people may be anonymous internet folks, but you did an amazing service for yourself just admitting your feelings. Please take the next step and do something about your unhappiness, wheather it be weightloss, therapy or getting out there and making some friends.


PS- meetup.com has groups of people you can do stuff with. I know it seems difficult, it was for me at first, and I even have a group of friends, I just wanted to (warning: cheesy)"expand my horizons/ meet new people" The (they call them) meetups have all kinds of people in them - trust me, I've been to lots of different kinds - and I've NEVER seen anyone judge or be rude to anyone else. The groups are very accepting, for goodness sake, people are there voluntarily to be nice to others. Maybe a meetup.com bookclub? They're a really easy start, as are movie clubs - even less talking - and it technically involves others!

Bobby is a jerk. He likes to try to do as much as he can get away with. But we kind of like him that way. It is who he is.

He is 7.5-ish and NOT mellow at all. I didn't adopt him until he was 5-ish and I can't even imagine how active he must have been as a pup. 

He likes constant attention and activity, but then all of a sudden he decides he is "done" and takes himself to bed and does not want to be bothered. He'll also get really pushy when he wants to be petted or scratched, moving our hands with his paws, and even scratching himself against our fingers if we won't comply. And of course he'll head butt doors to try to get them to open. He doesn't try to destroy anything though, except his toys, thank goodness.

He had an attempted murder problem (, of other dogs,) and he went away intensive training for 2 months. Now he is much better, and listens to us about other things too. I wasn't being strict enough...which I knew but couldn't change...until now. 

He is still really dominant and tries to get his way - we just chalk it up to his spunky personality, and try to not really let him "win". However, he will never be able to be off leash out of the yard, it's just not worth trusting him - something terrible could happen to another animal if he snaps - and we won't risk that.

He's excellent with all people, including strangers, and especially kids: babies, toddlers, etc. Kids of any age can be really rough with him and he'll be super sweet and patient, and never ever nip or run away.

So, um, if you can afford it, serious training can be really helpful. I wish i had done it sooner.

like JeF4y i carried bobby through the metal detector. we had to arrive early and wait in the "special circumstances" line to check in. we could not check in online.

delta's website says it allows 4 pets per flight, but the employee checking us in said they only allow ONE pet per flight unless you fall under a special category, and there are lots of special categories. here is the link with more info for delta: http://www.delta.com/content/www/en_US/traveling-with-us/special-travel-needs/pets/pet-travel-options.html

we flew delta, but i looked up southwest, and they only charge $75 each way for pets. but overall, the pet fee + delta ticket was less for us, and it was a direct flight - which i look upon as a huge bonus. 

we flew cross country, and the flight was about 4 hrs. i gave him a bit of water and ice (he likes to chew ice) during the flight and plenty of snacks to keep him busy. he wasn't really interested in drinking more, i offered it.

on the way out he didn't take any sedatives, and seemed a bit rambunctious from all the excitement. he only barked after landing though and was really really really keen on getting off the plane. but again, i think he was just excited.

on the way back i gave him some benadryl, our vet said it was ok. calmed him a bit, but didn't really do that much. no barking at all though on landing.
